## TL;DR

Task #1265 now exposes `humanTaskCheck.mode` (`keywords`, `model`, or `both`) and extra keyword phrases in Settings and TOML. The default mode is keyword-first; it invokes the configured decision provider only after a phrase hit. Model-only mode checks the whole task, with the keyword result as a fail-safe if the provider is unavailable. I connected the new mode through the server flag and start paths, made settings values round-trip through the browser config API, preserved explicitly configured legacy behavior, and narrowed the keyword tripwires.

Table-driven tests cover both Tiao #0175 criteria and the three human-gated examples in the task notes. The final focused human-step run passed 50 tests. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed on the final tree, including build, all scoped tests, UI smoke, contrast audit and user-docs checks.

## Work and rationale

The former matcher treated broad terms such as “device verification” and bare “credentials” as evidence that a person had to act. That created false positives for biometrics tested with fixtures, credential parsing, and criteria explicitly saying that no physical step was required. The core scan now masks code identifiers and inline code, ignores negated clauses, and uses more specific phrases for real-device checks, external sign-up, environment access, and a human supplying a secret. Project-specific phrases can be added one per line; the API accepts an empty list so a user can clear those additions.

The three-way setting lives in the shared Agents → Model routing panel. `both` runs the keyword check first and asks the configured decision provider only on a hit. `keywords` uses only phrase rules. `model` asks about the task even without a phrase match and retains the first acceptance criterion so a human verdict can quote the criterion. The model still uses the existing configured provider and timeout. Shadow mode only records a verdict; Automatic mode can block. If the model call fails, the start route and the asynchronous flag path state that the keyword result was used. In model-only mode, a failed check with no keyword hit does not create a refusal.

The browser config contract now flattens the new nested values, so the Settings controls show saved phrases after reload. The config schema uses a select for the mode, the phrase array is registered among supported keys, and the user configuration reference describes the setting. An explicitly configured old `model_routing.humanStepCheck = false` continues to mean keyword-only when the new mode is absent; a new explicit mode takes precedence.

Model calls continue through the existing decision adapter and record usage with session type `human-check`. Successful decisions are persisted against the task body fingerprint, preserving the existing restart-safe cache and invalidation on task edits. Refusal detail includes the quoted criterion and the bounded reason produced from the model’s structured answers.

## Approaches tried

I inspected the keyword assessment, both server paths that can stop a task, config parsing and browser flattening, the model provider abstraction, and the Model routing panel. Reusing the existing provider keeps network calls injectable in tests and avoids introducing a second provider path. I initially ran the focused tests against the narrower keywords; that exposed an old assertion requiring “API keys from disk” to flag. I changed it because discussing agent-doable key handling is not itself a human dependency, while the explicit “user pastes their secret key” case remains flagged.

I then checked the mode setting end-to-end and found that legacy boolean gates still prevented the new mode from taking effect. I changed those gates to resolve the new mode first, kept legacy fallback behavior, and added negative-fallback handling so a model outage cannot turn a no-keyword task into a refusal. A first broader focused run caught stale UI copy assertions after the compatibility toggle was relabeled; I updated that test to cover the new mode group and phrase editor.

## Challenges and blockers

The existing provider contract returns one task-level probability and bounded reason rather than independent verdict objects for every acceptance criterion. The implementation supplies the full task body and the matched criterion to the provider, and the displayed refusal quotes a criterion, but it does not yet create a separate persisted model verdict for each criterion. The existing provider routing settings also determine the model and backend; this change does not add a separate allowlist-backed agent role for the human-step check.

The first `repoos check` result failed formatting; I formatted the affected files and continued. The next remote run surfaced old model-gate tests that relied on an implicit `API keys` keyword. I updated those fixtures to configure their trigger phrase explicitly and to assert the required visible keyword fallback on model failure. Later remote checks passed the build and tests, but a local build guard timed out once and a local fallback exposed a timezone-sensitive date assertion plus a load-sensitive free-port case. I made the date assertion use the same locale formatting as the UI, verified the free-port test in isolation, and reran the full scoped check. Remote runners were unavailable on the final attempt, so the local fallback completed: all tests, UI smoke, contrast audit, and docs build passed. The pressure guard paused briefly before final gates and resumed without intervention.

## Key learnings

A useful human-step matcher needs action and context. “Credentials” can describe test fixtures, implementation, or a true dependency on a person. A negated requirement and an API identifier should not trigger the same path as a person signing up or supplying a secret. Tests need both classes of examples together so the check does not become accurate only by disabling important signals. Existing test fixtures also need to declare custom triggers explicitly instead of relying on broad legacy words.

Settings require a complete round trip: schema metadata and supported keys are only part of the feature. The parsed object must be flattened for the browser, and arrays need an explicit empty-list path if clearing them is a valid operation. Finally, every path that can refuse a start or set a persistent flag must share the same mode and fallback semantics; fixing only the start endpoint leaves later task sweeps inconsistent.
